job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Femi Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior site engineer for a construction firm in Setúbal, south of Lisbon. I start at seven on site in a hard hat, checking that the concrete and the steel match the drawings and writing the daily report. After lunch I'm in the portakabin doing measurements and emails. I studied civil engineering and passed, no internship, because I worked weekends on my uncle's building jobs. I rent a small flat with a cousin, and on Sundays I go to church with my mother and then to lunch at my grandmother's.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does your family think about the career, and how's the firm treating you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My father was a mason and he's proud, because I'm the first in the family to wear the engineer's helmet. The firm is run by Senhor Albuquerque, a serious man who works the old way: you learn by being on site and he checks your reports himself. My parents helped me with a deposit-sized amount in the bank, so money is not a worry. I don't use computers for more than I have to, and I've never used any AI. I prefer to see the wall myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's all noise. At work I'd tell Senhor Albuquerque that nothing replaces an engineer who walks the site. At church I'd say people should worry about real things, like rent and family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm relieved. I want to learn the work from the people who do it, and that is a slow path. If AI makes paperwork a bit faster, fine, but I can still do it by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, work toward my professional registration with the engineers' association and save 500 euros a month. I'd propose to Joana before the end of the year, and we'd plan a wedding in about 18 months. I'd keep going to Sunday lunch, because family is the reason for the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good, steady and a little proud. It's what I trained for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your site days change if the paperwork software got a bit better?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of the paperwork might shrink. I'd still check the site myself, because a measurement from a screen is not a measurement from the wall. If anything, a faster report gives me more time to walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still weigh on you in that quiet world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Housing. The rent is high in Setúbal, and if Joana and I marry and have children, a flat is expensive. My parents would help, but I'd hate to ask. I'd rather earn it with work than be given it.

say: It's all **noise**, because nothing replaces an engineer who walks the site.
People should worry about **real** things like rent and family.
think: I'm relieved, because I want to learn the work from people who do it, which is a **slow** path.
I can still do the paperwork by **hand**.
do: Work toward **professional registration** and save 500 euros a month.
Propose to **Joana** this year and plan a wedding in about 18 months.
S0.quote: A measurement from a screen is not a measurement from the wall.
fieldNote: His faith in **site** knowledge is the root of his calm.
Housing is the pressure; he would rather **earn** than be given help.
Family plans, marriage and a flat shape his idea of success.

steps.text: Apply for professional registration with the engineers' association
Save 500 euros a month for the wedding and a flat
Propose to Joana and plan the wedding for next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's another change we'll deal with, like any other. I'd tell friends that those who work with their hands and their heads will be fine. I'd say the young should learn a trade and not wait for handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm uneasy. The reports, the measurements log and the planning are things the software could do. My own job is half site and half desk, and the desk half is the one at risk. I fear the firm will say one engineer can do the work of two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend more time on site and take on safety inspection, since that needs a person with a helmet. I'd learn one new piece of software only when Senhor Albuquerque tells me to. I'd also take a short course on site safety law, about 400 euros.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not fear exactly. It's a feeling that the ground I stand on isn't as solid as my father's was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your tasks are most likely to go to software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The daily report, the quantity checks and scheduling. Those are the ones I do at the desk. What stays is deciding whether the formwork is safe, and standing next to the crane operator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Senhor Albuquerque do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's old-fashioned, but he's not stupid. He'd keep the people he trusts and make everyone learn the software. If I do what he says, I think he'd keep me. That's the kind of trust my father would have recognised.

say: It's another change we'll deal with, and those who work with **hands and heads** will be fine.
The young should learn a **trade** and not wait for handouts.
think: The reports, measurements log and planning could be done by **software**, and that's the desk half of my job.
The firm may say one engineer can do the work of **two**.
do: Spend more time on **site** and take on safety inspection.
Learn new software only when Senhor Albuquerque (my boss) **tells me**.
Take a short **site safety law** course for about 400 euros.
feel: **Uneasy**: the ground I stand on isn't as solid as my father's was.
S1.quote: What stays is deciding whether the formwork is safe, and standing next to the crane operator.
fieldNote: Knows which half of his job is **exposed** and which half is safe.
Resists new tools but accepts **orders** from a trusted boss.
Blames no one; his values lean on work, trade and self-reliance.

steps.text: Take on more site safety inspections
Pay for a short site safety law course
Learn the new reporting software only when ordered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after each other, family first, then the church and the neighbours. I'd say governments move too slowly, and ordinary people will have to hold things together. I'd also say we shouldn't simply hand out money, but give people real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious about the year 2028. If thinking AI does everything, the firm has no use for a junior who does desk tasks. Robots come around 2031, so site work stays three years longer, but that is not a career. I'm 22 and should be working for forty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save 900 euros a month and put off the wedding by a year, though that would hurt Joana. I'd ask the firm to move me fully onto site work. I'd go to my uncle about taking on building jobs together. I'd lean on the church group, who help with jobs and rooms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd pray more, and I'd be quieter at home. I wouldn't want Joana to see how afraid I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you deal with the first year, step by step?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, speak to Senhor Albuquerque honestly. Second, cut costs. Third, take every site hour offered. Fourth, talk to my uncle about a small business, so that if the firm stops, I still have something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father, my uncle and the priest, in that order. My father would say a man works with his hands. My uncle would say come and build with me. I'd feel ashamed that I needed it, but I'd do it.

say: We need to look after each other, **family** first, then the church and neighbours.
We shouldn't hand out money, but give people real **work**.
think: If thinking AI does everything, the firm has no use for a junior who does **desk** tasks.
Site work stays three years longer, but that's not a **career**.
do: Save **900 euros** a month and put off the wedding by a year.
Ask the firm to move me fully onto **site** work.
Talk to my **uncle** about building jobs together.
feel: **Anxious**; I'd pray more and hide how afraid I am from Joana.
S2.quote: Site work stays three years longer, but that is not a career. I'm 22 and should be working for forty years.
fieldNote: His **faith** and family network are real resources.
Delaying the wedding shows how far fear would reach into his life.
Wants work, not **handouts**, even when afraid.

steps.text: Save 900 euros a month and delay the wedding a year
Ask Senhor Albuquerque to move me fully onto site work
Start small building jobs with my uncle on weekends
Lean on the church group for help with work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to prepare, so use it well. I'd say people should learn trades and marry and build homes, not just wait. I'd tell the young at church to stop complaining and learn something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel uneasy but I can see a way. By 2031 I could be a fully registered site manager and a partner in a small building firm with my uncle. The robots arrive around 2034, but they'd need someone to run them on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my registration in two years and take a project management course. I'd build side jobs with my uncle on weekends, renovating flats. I'd marry my girlfriend Joana next year, because waiting for the world to settle means waiting forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steady. I'd feel I have a path, which is a gift. It would be a long road but a clear one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two would not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to do the wedding, the registration and a small business in the right order. Two years would have made me choose between them. In five I can do all three, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the state in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I don't like handouts. I'd want apprenticeship schemes and tax breaks for small building firms, so a young man can start a business without a big loan. Give people the chance to work and get out of the way.

say: We've got time to prepare, so people should learn trades, **marry** and build homes.
I'd tell the young at church to stop complaining and learn something **real**.
think: By 2031 I could be a registered site manager and **partner** in a small building firm.
Robots arrive around 2034, but someone must run them on **site**.
do: Finish my **registration** in two years and take a project management course.
Renovate flats with my **uncle** on weekends.
feel: **Uneasy** but steady, with a clear path.
S3.quote: I'd marry my girlfriend Joana next year, because waiting for the world to settle means waiting forever.
fieldNote: He turns **uncertainty** into a plan with order: wedding, registration, business.
Wants **apprenticeships** and tax breaks, consistent with traditional free-market views.
A clear path lowers his unease.

steps.text: Finish professional registration within two years
Take an evening project management course
Renovate flats with my uncle on weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing if people use it well. I'd say let's build things, teach apprentices and keep our families strong. I'd tell the church group to stop fearing and start preparing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel calm. By 32, I could have a firm, a family and a home. If AI arrives in 2036, I'd already be settled, and I'd be passing on what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become a registered engineer, set up a small firm with my uncle by 27 and take apprentices. I'd buy a home near my parents, and have children with Joana. I'd stick with my own methods, and only take new tools when the firm needs them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a normal life. Ten years is the most generous gift of the five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take more risks with the firm and not be so cautious. I'd start earlier, since a decade lets me. I'd also invest in a second property to rent out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own children about it one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them: learn to build and to fix, to pray and to stay together. The machines may do the thinking, but a family does the loving. I'd want them to have a trade in their hands and a person's heart.

say: Ten years is a **blessing** if people use it well, so let's build and teach apprentices.
The church group should stop fearing and start **preparing**.
think: By 32 I could have a firm, a **family** and a home.
If AI arrives in 2036, I'd already be **settled**.
do: Become a registered engineer and set up a small **firm** with my uncle by 27.
Buy a **home** near my parents and have children with Joana.
Take new tools only when the **firm** needs them.
feel: **Calm**; it feels like a normal life.
S4.quote: The machines may do the thinking, but a family does the loving.
fieldNote: The long runway makes his **traditional** plan feasible.
Wants to pass on skills as an **apprentice** teacher.

steps.text: Set up a small building firm with my uncle by age 27
Take on two apprentices from the local trade school
Buy a home near my parents and have children

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, without a doubt. I'd have no time to build what I have planned, and I'd be hurting Joana's plans too. What would help is family, the church and a chance to work, with apprenticeships and not handouts. And honesty from my firm.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against progress. I'm slow, and I like to see it work before I trust it. That is how my father built walls that are still standing.

headlineQuote: I'm slow, and I like to see it work before I trust it.
portrait: Femi is **22**, a junior site engineer in Setúbal, with a pass degree in civil engineering and no internship.
He is traditional, religious and free-market, trusts **family** and the church and never uses AI.
His job is half site and half desk, so he tries to shift toward the **hands-on** half.
Mood runs calm, uneasy, anxious, uneasy, calm, and he plans a **wedding** and a small firm.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he would have no time to build his **plans** or Joana's.
whatWouldHelp: **Family**, the church, apprenticeships and real work, and honesty from his firm.
